Quickstart: from documents to a model, in R

Source: vignettes/quickstart.Rmd
quickstart.Rmd

dragonfarm turns your material into a small language model that is yours: it answers in your domain and your voice, and it loads anywhere with plain transformers. This page walks the default route once, on the example documents that ship with the package: read documents, ask them questions, have a model write training questions, review them, fine-tune, compare. The same six steps are the tabs of the app (dragon_app()).

If your data is already a table of prompts and replies, skip to the table route at the end.

1. Check the machine 

library(dragonfarm)
dragon_check()

The first call builds a Python environment with torch and transformers. That is a 2 to 3 GB download and takes a few minutes; later calls take a second. The report names the device, whether 4-bit loading is available, and the model it will use by default to answer questions on this machine: a 1.5B model under 6 GB of GPU memory or on a CPU, a 3B at 6 to 8 GB, a 7B in 4-bit at 8 GB and up.

Keep your sets and runs somewhere permanent; by default they live under a temporary folder and vanish with the session:

options(dragonfarm.runs_dir = "~/dragonfarm_runs")

2. Read the documents 

docs <- dragon_documents(dragon_example_documents(), name = "policies")
docs
#> Document set policies
#> • returns-and-warranty.md: 3 chunks, 328 words
#> • connectivity-and-app.md: 3 chunks, 360 words
#> • orders-and-support.md: 3 chunks, 389 words
#> 9 chunks of about 170 words; index: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5

The example is three short Markdown files of support policies for a fictional smart-home company (the same company as the example tickets). Your own PDF, HTML, Word, text, and spreadsheet files, folders of them, and web pages work the same way: dragon_documents(c("policies/", "https://...")). Text is split into chunks that never cross a heading, each remembering its file and section, and embedded with a small model (downloaded once, about 130 MB). Reading the same set again re-reads only files that changed.

3. Ask 

ans <- dragon_ask(docs, "How long is the return window?")
ans
#> Any device can be returned within 30 days of delivery, opened or unopened, for a full refund [1].
#>
#> [1]* returns-and-warranty.md › Returns
#> [2]  returns-and-warranty.md › Damaged on arrival
#> [3]  orders-and-support.md › Cancelling an order
#> [4]  returns-and-warranty.md › Warranty
#> * cited in the answer. Excerpt text is in $sources$text.

The most relevant chunks go in front of the model as numbered excerpts, with an instruction to answer only from them and to cite them. The first question in a session loads the model (about a minute for a 7B in 4-bit); later ones take seconds. For many uses this step is the whole job: nothing is trained, and you can swap the documents and ask again. dragon_chat(documents = docs) does the same with memory across turns.

4. Write training questions, and review them 

qa <- dragon_questions(docs)
#> 27 questions written, 16 kept by the filters (59%). Review them before training.
qa

For every chunk a model writes three self-contained questions and answers them from that chunk alone; deterministic filters then mark pairs that are not grounded in the chunk, name things it does not, refer to “the passage”, or repeat another question. Nothing is thrown away: each pair has keep and a reason. On a CPU, pass a small generator such as generator = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct" and expect to keep few; on a GPU the default is the machine’s recommended model, and a stronger teacher such as dragon_llm_anthropic() keeps more.

Now read them. This is the step that decides whether the fine-tune is worth having: in our tests, roughly a fifth of the pairs that passed the filters were still wrong or trivial, and a model trained on unreviewed pairs learned to sound sure when it was wrong.

qa[!qa$keep, c("question", "reason")]     # what was rejected, and why
qa$keep[qa$id == "p0007"] <- TRUE          # rescue one you like
dragon_questions_save(qa)                  # decisions stay with the set

In the app this is the Teach card: tick and untick, Save decisions, Continue to Model.

5. Fine-tune 

ds <- dragon_questions_dataset(qa, docs)   # kept pairs, with retrieved excerpts in every prompt
run <- dragon_train(ds, "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct",
                    lora = dragon_lora(r = 8, alpha = 16),
                    args = dragon_train_args(epochs = 2, batch_size = 2, grad_accum = 4, max_seq_len = 1024),
                    wait = TRUE)

Each training prompt is the excerpts retrieved for that question, then the question; the answer is the response. The model learns the style and how to use excerpts, and the documents stay the source of truth, so they can change later without retraining. The 135M model trains on a CPU in a few minutes; on a GPU, Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is the better default. With wait = TRUE you get a progress bar; without it the function returns at once and dragon_status(run), dragon_progress(run), and dragon_wait(run) follow along. Runs survive the session: dragon_run("~/dragonfarm_runs/<id>") reopens one.

6. Compare and use 

dragon_ask(docs, "Can I return a device I have already set up?", model = run)
dragon_ask(docs, "Can I return a device I have already set up?", model = run, base = TRUE)   # what it started from
dragon_evaluate(run)                        # held-out loss and sample replies
chat <- dragon_chat(run, documents = docs)  # a conversation, answering from the documents
chat$say("A customer wants to return an opened device.")
dragon_merge(run, "models/policies-135m")   # a standalone model for plain transformers

A 135M model trained on sixteen pairs will not impress you; this run is to see the parts move. Use a bigger base model, your own documents, and a reviewed set of a few hundred pairs for a result you would keep. The measured numbers behind each step, and what to expect from each model size, are in From your documents to your model.

The table route

If your data already comes as rows of prompt and response, start from a table instead. The bundled example tickets have subject, body, and reply columns:

ds <- dragon_dataset(dragon_example_data()) |>
  dragon_map(prompt = "{subject}\n\n{body}", response = "reply")
dragon_preview(ds, n = 1)                   # the first row exactly as the model sees it
run <- dragon_train(ds, "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct", wait = TRUE)
dragon_generate(run, "Charged twice for Sentry doorbell\n\nMy card shows two charges for one order.")

dragon_map() takes column names or templates that combine columns, and an optional system =. Everything after that is the same: evaluate, chat, merge, publish. In the app, “Have a table of prompts and replies instead?” on the Documents tab switches to this route, where the Map step is drag and drop.

Choosing settings

Model. Start with HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct or Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Move up only if quality is not enough; for answering from documents, a bigger base model with retrieval often beats a small fine-tuned one.

Rank. 8 to 16 is plenty for format and tone. Go to 32 or 64 when the model must learn a lot of new facts.

Learning rate. 2e-4 for LoRA. Halve it if the loss curve is jagged.

Epochs. 2 to 3. Watch the eval loss: if it rises while training loss falls, stop earlier.

Sequence length. Long enough for your longest prompt plus reply; document prompts with four excerpts need about 1024 tokens. Shorter is faster and uses less memory.

Out of memory? Lower batch_size, raise grad_accum to compensate, and turn on gradient_checkpointing.
